name: Erythrulose

card.summary: A raspberry-derived sugar used alongside DHA in self-tanners; claims rest on cosmetic-industry descriptions, with no trials found.
card.note: No published clinical studies of tanning performance found.

quick.overview:
Erythrulose is a small sugar used in sunless tanning products, usually together with DHA. It is described as giving a gradual, bronze-toned colour.
No clinical studies of its tanning effect were found.
quick.mechanism: It is described as reacting with amino acids in the outer skin layer (a Maillard-type reaction) to form brown pigments, more slowly than DHA.
quick.risks: No safety or regulatory data specific to erythrulose are available.

lead: Erythrulose is a four-carbon sugar used in sunless tanning products to give skin a gradual brown colour without sun exposure, so the wearer can look tanned without UV exposure. It is usually blended with dihydroxyacetone (DHA) in self-tanners, where it is used to build colour and help the tan look more natural and even.[1][3] It occurs naturally in fruits such as red raspberries and melons and is commonly produced by microbial fermentation.[1][2]

As a tanner, erythrulose is described as reacting with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a Maillard-type reaction, producing brown pigments without changing skin melanin. It develops more slowly than DHA, and the colour fades over days as the skin sheds.[3] Brands combine the two to reduce streaking and orange tones associated with DHA alone, according to Grokipedia.[1]

A 2026 review of sunless tanners found that all 37 of the top-selling products it examined contained DHA and 38 percent also contained erythrulose; about 2 percent of customer reviews mentioned skin reactions.[4] No clinical trials of erythrulose alone were found.

angle.text: Erythrulose adds a tan-coloured tint to the skin's surface, typically in a blend with DHA, giving a sun-free bronze that develops gradually.

infobox: Sunless tanning ingredient, often with DHA [1][3]

paras: Erythrulose appears in lotions, mousses, drops and sprays for the face and body. Because it develops over a longer period than DHA, it is described as giving a more gradual, even build-up of colour, and DHA/erythrulose blends are marketed for a more natural-looking bronze with less of the orange tone that early self-tanners were known for [1][3]. The 2026 review of top-selling products found erythrulose in 38 percent of 37 products and DHA in all of them [4].

Erythrulose is the only ketotetrose, with the formula C4H8O4 and a molar mass of about 120 g/mol. It exists as D and L forms, is a colourless, sweet-tasting, water-soluble compound, and can be made by enzyme-mediated condensation of glycolaldehyde.[1][2] In 2026 it was reported in a molecular cloud near the centre of the Milky Way.[2]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference that may contain errors, says erythrulose reacts with amino groups in keratin to form brown pigments (melanoidins), reacts more slowly than DHA, and is blended with DHA to improve evenness and wear; it is supplied as an aqueous syrup of about 80 percent active material.[1] Wikipedia's article on sunless tanning likewise says erythrulose works similarly to DHA but develops more slowly and is often included alongside it, with the tan fading over roughly 3 to 10 days.[3]

Wikipedia describes DHA as not a dye or stain: it reacts with amino acids in the outermost layer of dead skin cells in a Maillard-type browning reaction, and erythrulose behaves similarly but more slowly [3]. Because only the outer layer is involved, the colour fades over roughly 3 to 10 days as that layer sheds, and spray tans are described as lasting about 5 to 10 days [3].

Sunless tanning grew out of observations in the 1950s by Eva Wittgenstein at Cincinnati Children's Hospital that oral DHA stained skin brown. The first commercial DHA self-tanner, Man-Tan, launched in 1959, followed by Coppertone's Quick Tan in 1960. Early products were associated with an orange tone, and reformulation together with spray-tan booths expanded the market from the late 1990s [3]. Erythrulose later became a common companion ingredient [3].

Erythrulose occurs naturally in fruits such as red raspberries [2]. Industrially, the L form can be produced by microbial oxidation of the sugar alcohol meso-erythritol, with research describing membrane-bound dehydrogenases of acetic acid bacteria such as Gluconobacter oxydans [7][6]. It has also been identified as a degradation product of ascorbic acid under physiological conditions [8].

Wikipedia's sunless tanning article reports that DHA and erythrulose can both cause contact dermatitis, that the tan itself gives no sun protection, and that the US FDA has approved DHA for external use but not around the eyes, lips or mucous membranes or by inhalation.[3] The 2026 review lists contact dermatitis and pigmentary changes among reported adverse effects of sunless tanners generally.[4]

The tan provides no sun protection. Wikipedia cites a 2007 study reporting that skin treated with high levels of DHA produced more free radicals under sun exposure than untreated skin, and a 2010 EU scientific committee opinion that concluded DHA spray tanning posed no risk, an opinion that some specialists have criticised as relying on unpublished industry-linked studies [3].

No studies found testing erythrulose by itself. A 2026 review of sunless tanners examined product ingredients and customer reviews rather than clinical outcomes.[4] A 2017 French article on self-tanning products covers the category.[5]

timeline.event: First commercial DHA self-tanner, Man-Tan, appears; erythrulose later becomes a common companion ingredient.[3]
